title: Special Moves
subtitle: Castling, en passant, and pawn promotion.

steps.say: Chess has three special moves that break the normal rules. The first is castling: king and rook move TOGETHER — the king hops two squares toward a rook, and the rook jumps to the other side. It's the only move where two pieces move at once, and it's how your king finds shelter.

steps.prompt: The path is clear — castle kingside!
hints: Castling needs empty squares between king and rook, and neither may have moved before.
Tap the king, then the g1 square — king to g1, rook to f1, all in one move.

line.say: Castled! Your king now sits safely behind a wall of pawns, and the rook joined the game — two birds, one move.

rejections.say: That walks the king into the open — and once the king moves, you lose the right to castle forever! Castling does the job better.

steps.wrongSay: This is the moment to castle — king two squares toward the h1 rook.
steps.successSay: Rule of thumb: castle early, almost every game.

hints: Queenside castling: the king goes two squares toward the a1 rook.
King lands on c1, rook swings around to d1.

line.say: Long castle! The king tucks away on c1 and the rook lands on the strong central d-file immediately.

rejections.say: That's kingside — perfectly legal, but this challenge is about the LONG version: king to c1, rook to d1.

steps.wrongSay: Castle queenside: move the king two squares toward the a1 rook.
steps.successSay: Both castles mastered. Long castling often signals an aggressive, opposite-side attack game!

steps.say: Special move number two: en passant — French for 'in passing'. Watch what happens when a pawn tries to sneak past yours with a double step.

autoMoves.say: Black's pawn jumps two squares, trying to slip past your e5 pawn...
En passant! Your pawn captures it AS IF it had only moved one square. This is only allowed immediately — wait one move and the chance is gone forever.

steps.prompt: Black's f-pawn just double-stepped past you. Capture it en passant!
hints: Your e5 pawn may capture the f5 pawn as if it had moved only one square.
Capture diagonally onto f6 — the f5 pawn disappears.

line.say: En passant! The passing pawn is removed even though you landed 'behind' it. One of the strangest and prettiest rules in chess.

rejections.say: You pushed past — and the en passant right vanishes the instant you play anything else. It's now or never!

steps.wrongSay: Capture diagonally onto f6 — en passant only works right away.
steps.successSay: En passant: rarely available, deeply satisfying, and now in your toolkit.

steps.prompt: Promotion time — but careful: a queen here is a DRAW! Find the winning promotion.
hints: Try to picture the position after c8=Q: does the black king have any legal move? Is he in check? That combination is stalemate!
Promote to the piece that keeps control but leaves the king a square — the rook wins.

line.say: Underpromotion! The rook controls the back rank but leaves a6 free, so no stalemate — and rook versus king is an easy win. Sometimes LESS is more.

rejections.say: STALEMATE! The new queen covers every square around the king — a6, b6, b8, a8 — but he's not in check. Draw. This is the classic case for underpromotion.
No need to retreat — the pawn can promote right now. The only question is: which piece?

steps.wrongSay: Promote the pawn — but think about what each piece does to the cornered king.
steps.successSay: You just made a master-level decision: underpromoting to avoid stalemate. Beautiful.
